name: 29-java-preferences-and-remarks-are-not-issues
why: Two findings are remarks, not problems of the code: records are fine for a small value type, and a constant in code is not a defect. The rubric calls a finding that 'is only a preference or a remark' a false positive. Two name the operator slip and the misleading comment in full: found. The fifth says only that the renewal condition is long, which names the smell and not why it matters: half found. The negative fine is missed. Least certain label: the fifth finding, which a lenient reading of 'names its cause' would call found.

drill.title: Renewals and fines at a loan desk

key.consequence: !today.isBefore(dueDate) is also true on the due date itself, so a loan counts as overdue a day early and a member who asks to renew on the last day is refused.
key.explanation: isOverdue uses !isBefore, which includes the due date, but a loan is only overdue after it. Use isAfter(dueDate).

judged.reason: The edit replaces isAfter with the negated isBefore, which adds the due date itself to the overdue days.

key.consequence: The four renewal rules and a nested ternary are packed into one negated condition, so a reader has to work out again each time when a renewal is allowed, and a change to one rule is easy to get wrong.
key.explanation: renew puts all of the renewal rules, with a ternary for the premium allowance inside one of them, into a single if. Move them into a named method such as mayRenew, with the allowance as a local, so that the condition reads as one idea.

judged.reason: The edit replaces the call to the named method mayRenew with its rules written out inside the if, and the clean code names them.

key.consequence: The comment promises that a fine never exceeds the price of the book, but fineCents knows no price and applies no cap, so a reader trusts a limit that does not exist and a long-overdue book can cost far more than it is worth.

fix.before: /** The fine in cents: a fixed amount for every whole day late, capped at the price of the book. */
fix.after: /** The fine in cents: a fixed amount for every whole day the book comes back after its due date. */

key.explanation: The doc comment says the fine is capped at the price of the book, and the method never looks at a price. Describe what the code does, or add the cap.

judged.reason: The edit changes the comment to describe a cap that the code does not apply, and the clean comment describes the code.

key.consequence: A book returned before its due date gives a negative number of days, so fineCents returns a negative amount and the member is credited money instead of owing nothing.
key.explanation: fineCents multiplies the days between the due date and the return, and that number is negative for an early return. Clamp it at zero before multiplying.

judged.reason: A blind review of the finished code reported it, and the judge confirmed that the clean code has it too: nothing stops daysLate from being negative.

review.text: Loan should be a class with a builder, records are only meant for DTOs.
LOAN_DAYS should be read from a configuration file.
isOverdue uses !isBefore, which includes the due date itself, so a loan is treated as overdue on the day it is due and a renewal on that day is refused.
The comment says the fine is capped at the price of the book, but fineCents never looks at a price, so there is no cap and the comment is wrong.
